questions.q: What expensive problem do intent locks exist to avoid?
options: Having to scan every individual row for a conflicting lock before granting a table-level lock
Having to retry a transaction automatically after a deadlock
Having to recompile a stored procedure on every execution
Having to convert a shared lock to an exclusive lock
questions.explain: Without intent locks, SQL Server would have to check every row in a table to know whether a table-level request conflicts with something held below.

questions.q: What does an Intent Exclusive (IX) lock at the table level actually represent?
options: A signal that an exclusive lock is held on some row or page underneath that table, not a lock on the table's data itself
An exclusive lock on every row in the table
A shared lock that applies only to intent-based queries
A lock that prevents the table's schema from changing
questions.explain: Intent locks are flags at a higher level signaling that a real lock exists somewhere below, not locks on the data at that higher level.

questions.q: What does SIX (Shared with Intent Exclusive) represent?
options: A shared lock on the whole resource, combined with intent to take exclusive locks on specific rows or pages within it
Six separate shared locks held simultaneously
An exclusive lock that also grants read access to other sessions
A schema stability lock combined with a shared lock
questions.explain: SIX combines a table-wide shared lock (for reading the whole table) with intent to exclusively lock parts of it.

questions.q: Why is checking an IX lock at the table level cheaper than scanning every row?
options: Because the intent lock gives a constant-time answer about whether a conflict exists below, without inspecting individual rows
Because IX locks are stored in a separate, faster database
Because scanning rows is only slow on tables larger than 1 million rows
It isn't actually cheaper — SQL Server still scans every row regardless
questions.explain: Seeing an IX lock at the table level is enough information to know a conflict exists below, turning a row-by-row scan into one quick check.

questions.q: In sys.dm_tran_locks, while a transaction holds a row-level X lock inside a table, what else will typically appear for that same transaction?
options: A row with resource_type = 'OBJECT' and request_mode = 'IX' for the table itself
Nothing else — only the row-level lock is ever recorded
A Sch-M lock on the table
A U lock on every other row in the table
questions.explain: The intent lock at the table level accompanies the row-level lock, signaling that something below it is locked.
